one_liner: Book microbenchmark of musttail tail recursion against loops and plain recursion; shows parity, no speedup from musttail.
what_it_does: A companion sample for the Packt book Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (Chapter13/optimization/main_1.cpp) that times three versions each of factorial and Fibonacci over uint64_t with Google Benchmark: a loop, plain recursion, and an accumulator-passing tail recursion whose self-call carries [[clang::musttail]] through a feature-tested macro. It is a teaching benchmark, not a library; the reusable piece is the macro pattern for requesting a guaranteed tail call portably. Arguments are 32768 and 65536 for factorial and 16 and 32 for Fibonacci.
how_it_is_fast: It is not faster. musttail makes the compiler emit the recursive call as a jump or refuse to compile, so stack use stays constant at any depth; in the book's Release-build run the tail-recursive versions time like the loops (Fibonacci(32) about 6.94 ns versus 6.74 ns), consistent with the optimizer already eliminating these self tail calls. The large Fibonacci gap comes from replacing exponential double recursion with a linear accumulator, an algorithm change. Guaranteed tail calls pay off in interpreter dispatch instead: wasm3's interpreter notes describe operations that end by calling the next one so the compiler tail-call optimizes them and virtual registers map to CPU registers.
when_to_use: Deep recursion that must not grow the stack even in Debug or -O0 builds, where the optimizer would not turn the tail call into a jump.

Tail-call-threaded interpreters or parsers (one handler per opcode that ends by calling the next), where a guaranteed jump keeps state in registers and the stack flat; wasm3 is a catalogued interpreter built in this style.
You want a compile error rather than silent stack growth when a refactor moves the recursive call out of tail position.
As a copyable feature-test pattern: test __has_cpp_attribute(clang::musttail), then musttail, else expand to nothing.
when_not_to_use: As a speed optimization for self-recursive functions in optimized builds: every same-algorithm row in this benchmark shows parity with the loop.
MSVC and GCC before 15: the macro expands to nothing, so the musttail variant is ordinary recursion that depends on the optimizer (MSVC still builds the optimization_1 target).
Calls whose signature does not match the caller's or that are not in tail position: musttail cannot apply and compilation fails.
When the cost is algorithmic: naive double-recursive Fibonacci is slow because of its exponential call count, which no call-convention change fixes.

integration.form: source-drop (a feature-test macro plus an attribute on the return statement)
integration.dependencies: none for the technique; the benchmark needs Google Benchmark 1.9.4 via Conan 2
integration.min_toolchain: A compiler with [[clang::musttail]]: Clang, or GCC 15, whose C-family frontends implement [[clang::musttail]] and [[gnu::musttail]] per a search snippet of the GCC 15.1 release announcement (page not reachable); the target builds as cxx_std_20 with the repo's GCC 15 Conan profile and CMake 3.28
integration.platforms: any target where the compiler can emit the tail call; the attribute is non-standard
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (pure functions with no shared state)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the one-argument wrappers keep the loop's signature, but inside they are accumulator-passing rewrites, not the naive double recursion they are compared against

gotchas: Every benchmarked factorial result is 0: n! for n of 66 or more holds at least 64 factors of 2, so the uint64_t product wraps to zero at 32768 and 65536; the timings still measure the multiply chain, but the outputs are meaningless.

iteration::fibonacci(1) returns 0 because its loop never runs, and tail_recursion::factorial(0) wraps n to 4294967295 and recurses about 4.3 billion times because it stops only at n == 1; neither input is benchmarked.
The macro is named musttail, so any header included after it that spells [[gnu::musttail]] or __attribute__((musttail)) gets rewritten; use a prefixed name when copying the pattern.

The harness runs only Release builds and shallow depths (32 calls for Fibonacci, 65536 for factorial), so it never shows musttail's real benefit, bounded stack use where the optimizer would not eliminate the call.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: It does not compete with the VM siblings; read it as a primer on guaranteed tail calls, then look at wasm3, whose interpreter is built on operations that tail-call the next one, or at the same repo's computed-goto versus switch dispatch entry, which is the actual interpreter-dispatch measurement in this book's code.
verified_claims_summary: No speedup from musttail was measured: the book's own run, relayed by the seed lead and not on any repo page, has iterative, plain-recursive and tail-recursive factorial of 32768 and 65536 all at about 20 to 40 microseconds and tail-recursive Fibonacci(32) at about 6.94 ns against 6.74 ns iterative; naive double-recursive Fibonacci(32) at about 2.39 ms differs only because it is exponential-time. Compiler, flags and hardware for that run are not stated; the repo builds optimization_1 as a C++20 CMake Release target with a GCC 15/libstdc++ Conan profile.
status_note: Active Packt companion repository (last commit 2026-09-27, mostly README edits; CI builds only Chapter10/customer, not this benchmark), MIT-licensed; the macro is small enough to copy but brings no speed in optimized builds.
